title: Minimal Data, Maximum Clarity: A Heuristic for Explaining Optimization (Rayegan & Menzies, arXiv:2509.08667v2)

edges.target: SMAC (Hutter et al.; SMAC3 package)
edges.ref: [49] F. Hutter, H. H. Hoos, K. Leyton-Brown, Sequential model-based optimization for general algorithm configuration, LION 2011; [50] Lindauer et al., SMAC3, JMLR 2022
edges.evidence: EZR is ranked in the best statistical group for nearly all datasets, while SMAC lags significantly under this tight budget.

edges.target: DEHB (Awad, Mallik, Hutter)
edges.ref: [43] N. Awad, N. Mallik, F. Hutter, Dehb: Evolutionary hyperband for scalable, robust and efficient hyperparameter optimization, arXiv:2105.09821 (2021)
edges.evidence: All methods (EZR, SMAC, DEHB, and Random) were restricted to the same number of objective evaluations to ensure fairness.

edges.target: LIME (Ribeiro et al.)
edges.ref: [33] M. T. Ribeiro, S. Singh, C. Guestrin, "Why should I trust you?" explaining the predictions of any classifier, KDD 2016
edges.evidence: For this instance, we generate explanations using three widely adopted techniques: LIME, SHAP, and BreakDown. In contrast, EZR provides local explanations natively.

edges.target: SHAP (Lundberg & Lee)
edges.ref: [34] S. M. Lundberg, S.-I. Lee, A unified approach to interpreting model predictions, NeurIPS 2017
edges.evidence: only SHAP consistently outperforms EZR in these higher thresholds, yet it does so with full supervision, whereas EZR achieves comparable performance using only 150 labels.

edges.target: BreakDown (Staniak & Biecek)
edges.ref: [35] M. Staniak, P. Biecek, Explanations of model predictions with live and breakdown packages, The R Journal (2018)
edges.evidence: For BreakDown, Figure 9, the prediction builds sequentially from the baseline 0.454 to 0.500.

edges.target: ReliefF (Robnik-Sikonja & Kononenko)
edges.ref: [55] M. Robnik-Sikonja, I. Kononenko, An adaptation of relief for attribute estimation in regression, ICML'97
edges.evidence: Using this same k, all other methods are applied to select their respective top-k features. Each resulting feature subset is then used to train the LGBM regression model

edges.target: ANOVA feature filter
edges.ref: [56] L. St, S. Wold, et al., Analysis of variance (anova), Chemometrics and intelligent laboratory systems (1989)
edges.evidence: We compare three commonly used methods in the SE domain, ReliefF, SHAP, ANOVA, alongside using all features, and EZR.

edges.target: Regression baselines: LR, Random Forest, SVR, ANN, LightGBM
edges.ref: [48] L. Breiman, Random forests, Machine learning (2001) (only RF is cited; LR/SVR/ANN/LGBM uncited)
edges.evidence: Linear Regression(LR) was chosen to represent classic statistical models, while Random Forest(RF) serves as a representative of tree-based ensemble methods. Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM or LGBM)

edges.target: LightGBM (downstream learner / explained model)
edges.ref: no reference entry; named in text as 'Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM or LGBM)'
edges.evidence: Each of the methods is paired with the LightGBM regressor across all datasets

edges.target: Scott-Knott test
edges.ref: [57] A. J. Scott, M. Knott, A cluster analysis method for grouping means in the analysis of variance, Biometrics (1974); adopted 'as used in' [21] Senthilkumar & Menzies, [58] Ganguly & Menzies
edges.evidence: While statistical rank-based methods such as Scott-Knott [57], as used in [21, 58], offer a way to group treatments by significance

edges.target: Cohen's small-effect rule (Cohen)
edges.ref: [61] J. Cohen, A power primer. (2016).
edges.evidence: Cohen's rule [61] stats that results are statistically distinguishable if they differ by more than a "small effect" ... 0.35 is the border between small and medium

edges.target: Hamlet's Probable Correctness Theory (geometric sampling bound)
edges.ref: [60] R. G. Hamlet, Probable correctness theory, Information processing letters (1987)
edges.evidence: the probability of drawing an epsilon-optimal solution follows a geometric distribution. The number of samples needed to achieve confidence C ... 1 - (1 - epsilon)^n >= C

edges.target: Ganguly & Menzies 'Bingo' (50-label plateau)
edges.ref: [58] K. K. Ganguly, T. Menzies, Bingo! simple optimizers win big if problems collapse to a few buckets (2025)
edges.evidence: This choice of 50 iterations follows the finding by Ganguly and Menzies [58] that most datasets reach state-of-the-art performance at this point.

edges.target: Ganguly & Menzies 'Bingo' 50-label plateau, re-checked by budget sensitivity analysis
edges.ref: [58] K. K. Ganguly, T. Menzies, Bingo! simple optimizers win big if problems collapse to a few buckets (2025)
edges.evidence: Budgets below the selected defaults are frequently and significantly worse, whereas increasing the budget beyond the selected defaults rarely produces statistically distinguishable improvements.
edges.section: 5.1.1 ('to validate the theoretical budget in practice'); 6.1 item 3, Figs 13-14

edges.target: MOOT repository (Menzies & Chen)
edges.ref: [59] T. Menzies, T. Chen, Moot repository of multi-objective optimization tests (2025). URL http://github.com/timm/moot
edges.evidence: This study uses datasets from the MOOT repository (Multi-Objective Optimization Testing) [59] ... In total, we used 60 datasets categorized under five main types in MOOT

edges.target: COC1000 dataset (MOOT, COCOMO-style process model)
edges.ref: https://github.com/timm/moot/blob/master/optimize/process/coc1000.csv (COCOMO origin: [26] B. W. Boehm, Software engineering economics)
edges.evidence: consider the COC1000 dataset from the MOOT repository. This dataset models a COCOMO-style software process

edges.target: Permutation importance framework (Biecek & Burzykowski)
edges.ref: [32] P. Biecek, T. Burzykowski, Explanatory model analysis: explore, explain, and examine predictive models, Chapman and Hall/CRC, 2021
edges.evidence: In this study, we employ the permutation importance framework [32], a model-agnostic technique that quantifies each feature's contribution by permuting its values

edges.target: Alcaide et al. (permutation importance for XAI in SE)
edges.ref: [64] F. J. Alcaide, J. R. Romero, A. Ramirez, Can explainable artificial intelligence support software modelers in model comprehension?, SoSyM (2025)
edges.evidence: Following Alcaide et al. [64], who demonstrated its utility for configuration-error detection, we use this approach to benchmark EZR.

edges.target: Mean Decrease in Impurity (Breiman, Random Forests)
edges.ref: [48] L. Breiman, Random forests, Machine learning (2001)
edges.evidence: summing its impurity reductions across the tree, directly aligning with the Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI) framework used in tree-based models such as Random Forests [48]

edges.target: XAI-as-feature-selection evaluation protocol (Arreche; Hinterleitner; Marcilio & Eler)
edges.ref: [52] Arreche et al., arxiv:2410.10050; [53] Hinterleitner et al., arxiv:2409.16787; [54] Marcilio & Eler, SIBGRAPI 2020
edges.evidence: we adopt a complementary approach inspired by recent XAI evaluations in other domains [52-54] ... whether its feature-importance rankings can improve downstream predictive performance

edges.target: Hoffman et al. explanation triggers (XAI metrics)
edges.ref: [65] R. R. Hoffman, S. T. Mueller, G. Klein, J. Litman, Metrics for explainable ai: Challenges and prospects, arxiv:1812.04608 (2018)
edges.evidence: Table 9: Common explanation triggers and associated user goals in XAI systems [65] ... We evaluate how well the cohort-based explanation addresses each practitioner question

edges.target: Pearl's Ladder of Causation
edges.ref: [47] J. Pearl, D. Mackenzie, The book of why: the new science of cause and effect, Basic books, 2018
edges.evidence: Within Pearl's Ladder of Causation, EZR spans all three rungs ... whereas attribution methods remain confined to associations.

edges.target: Chebyshev distance as alternative multi-objective metric
edges.ref: [21] L. Senthilkumar, T. Menzies, Can LLMs improve SE active learning via warm-starts? (2024); [67] Giagkiozis & Fleming, Methods for multi-objective optimization, Inf. Sci. (2015)
edges.evidence: we repeated all experiments using the Chebyshev distance [21, 67]. While absolute scores differed, the relative rankings and overall conclusions remained stable.

edges.target: Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE)
edges.ref: [44] S. Watanabe, Tree-structured parzen estimator: Understanding its algorithm components..., arxiv:2304.11127 (2023); [10] Bergstra & Bengio, JMLR 2012
edges.evidence: EZR is inspired by TPE, which models good and bad configurations using Parzen estimators ... EZR simplifies this process by using a Naive Bayes classifier

edges.target: Hoare quickselect (Algorithm 65: find)
edges.ref: [46] C. A. Hoare, Algorithm 65: find, Communications of the ACM (1961)
edges.evidence: Hoare's Quickselect pivot-and-partition strategy [46], both of which support the use of small but statistically meaningful sampling budgets in optimization and explanation tasks.

edges.target: PROMISETUNE (Chen & Chen): best solutions cluster in a tiny region of the Pareto front
edges.ref: [20] P. Chen, T. Chen, Promisetune: Unveiling causally promising and explainable configuration tuning, arXiv:2507.05995 (2025)
edges.evidence: The PROMISETUNE [20] study reports that the best solutions are typically clustered into a very small region of the total Pareto frontier.
edges.section: 2.1 (justifies avoiding hypervolume/spread/GD/IGD; 'Inspired by the PROMISETUNE results')

edges.target: Lustosa & Menzies DRR (low intrinsic dimensionality of SE data)
edges.ref: [25] A. Lustosa, T. Menzies, Less noise, more signal: Drr for better optimizations of se tasks, arxiv:2503.21086 (2025); [45] Menzies & Lustosa, arXiv:2405.12920
edges.evidence: Dimensionality Reduction Ratio (DRR) study shows that a small fraction of intrinsic dimensions captures nearly all the variability in software engineering performance metrics [25].

edges.target: Agrawal et al. (intrinsic dimensionality threshold I < 5 -> simpler optimizers)
edges.ref: [42] A. Agrawal, X. Yang, R. Agrawal, R. Yedida, X. Shen, T. Menzies, Simpler hyperparameter optimization for software analytics: Why, how, when?, IEEE TSE 48(8) (2021) 2939-2954
edges.evidence: Agrawal et al. [42] proposed using intrinsic dimensionality thresholds (I < 5) to select between simple and complex optimizers ... EZR operationalizes this principle

edges.target: Lustosa & Menzies iSNEAK (small-budget derivation from Hamlet/Hoare)
edges.ref: [62] A. Lustosa, T. Menzies, isneak: Partial ordering as heuristics for model-based reasoning in software engineering, IEEE Access (2024)
edges.evidence: Similar theoretical reasoning has been employed by Lustosa et al. [62] in their partial-ordering explanations, drawing from Hamlet's Probable Correctness Theory [60] and Hoare's Quickselect

edges.target: Sayagh et al.: over 60% of configuration variables never changed after creation
edges.ref: [3] M. Sayagh, N. Kerzazi, B. Adams, F. Petrillo, Software configuration engineering in practice: interviews, survey, and systematic literature review, IEEE TSE (2018)
edges.evidence: empirical data shows that over 60% of configuration variables remain unchanged after their initial creation, highlighting how rarely these options are actively optimized [3].

edges.target: Miller's magical number seven (limited cognitive capacity)
edges.ref: [37] G. A. Miller, The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information, Psychol. Rev. (1956); via [36] Chen, Fu, Krishna, Menzies, FSE 2018
edges.evidence: humans have limited cognitive capacity, as noted by Miller's "magical number seven" [37]. Stakeholders cannot reason about hundreds of variables simultaneously.
edges.section: 2.2 Explainable AI in SE (justifies small trees / few features)

edges.target: Nair et al. FLASH: labeling cost dominates; GP-based Bayesian optimization scales poorly
edges.ref: [18] V. Nair, Z. Yu, T. Menzies, N. Siegmund, S. Apel, Finding faster configurations using flash, IEEE TSE (2018)
edges.evidence: This stands in contrast to methods like DEHB [43], which require thousands of evaluations, or traditional Bayesian optimization with Gaussian Process Models that scale poorly with dataset size [18].

edges.target: Pareto quality-indicator evaluation (hypervolume/spread/GD/IGD; Li, Chen & Yao; Chen & Li; Nair et al.)
edges.ref: [19] M. Li, T. Chen, X. Yao, How to evaluate solutions in Pareto-based SBSE, IEEE TSE (2020); [22][23] T. Chen, M. Li (FSE 2024; TOSEM 2023); [24] Nair, Agrawal, Chen, Fu, Mathew, Menzies, Minku, Wagner, Yu, MSR 2018
edges.evidence: traditional assessment methods (hypervolume, spread, GD, IGD) are highly misleading since those measures comment on the whole frontier (and not the tiny regions containing the best solutions).
edges.section: 2.1 (rejects Pareto-front metrics in favour of d2h)

edges.target: Palacio et al.: causal inference for interpreting code models
edges.ref: [66] D. N. Palacio, A. Velasco, N. Cooper, A. Rodriguez, K. Moran, D. Poshyvanyk, Toward a theory of causation for interpreting neural code models, IEEE TSE (2024)
edges.evidence: Building on prior work advocating the integration of causal inference into software engineering [66], we also evaluate EZR through Pearl's Ladder of Causation [47]

edges.target: Mohammadkhani et al.: subjective XAI assessments overlook objective utility
edges.ref: [27] A. H. Mohammadkhani et al., A systematic literature review of explainable ai for software engineering, arxiv:2302.06065 (2023)
edges.evidence: such evaluations, though valuable, may overlook more objective measures of explanatory utility [27]. To address this limitation, we adopt a complementary approach
